Headline: Finland celebrates 108th Independence Day with traditions, tensions
Full_Text: Finland marked its Independence Day on Saturday with the usual mix of solemn ceremonies, community events and political demonstrations, some of which required heavy police presence in central Helsinki. Yle News reporter Matthew Schilke explained some of Finland's Independence Day traditions in the video below. The day's official commemorations began in Helsinki, where President Alexander Stubb and his spouse Suzanne Innes-Stubb laid a wreath at the Hietaniemi Cemetery's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Despite steady rain, hundreds of people gathered to watch the ceremony, which concluded with a military band playing the national anthem. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) and representatives of the Defence Forces, the Border Guard, veterans' organisations and the City of Helsinki also laid wreaths. Elsewhere, Kouvola hosted the national Independence Day parade, attracting large crowds along Salpausselänkatu. The march was reviewed by Lieutenant General Kim Jäämeri, Finland's military representative to the EU and Nato. In Helsinki, the traditional Heikki Hursti's meal for the disadvantaged drew long queues despite the rain. Volunteers served free soup to around 800 people, continuing the decades-long charity tradition founded by Veikko and Toimi Hursti. A second tradition — begun only last year — saw Helsinki cold-water swimmers gather again in Jätkäsaari to sing Finlandia while wading in the frigid sea. Independence Day also brought a series of politically charged marches and counter-protests, particularly in Helsinki's Töölö district, prompting significant transport disruptions on tram and bus lines throughout the afternoon and evening. The first major event was the "Suomi herää" ("Finland Awakens") march, which departed from Railway Square with around 500 masked participants, including members of the far-right Active Club network. Participants lit pyrotechnic torches, at times filling Mannerheimintie with thick smoke. Police said the burning flares caused safety risks in the crowd, and officers intervened in the actions of at least two people. One man who attempted to block the procession shouted "shame on you!" before police removed him from the route. The march ended outside the Finnish Parliament Building, where police stood guard. Later in the evening, authorities fenced off Töölöntori, the traditional starting point for the 612 torchlight march, which has in past years included far-right participants. Police expect tensions as the counter-movement "Helsinki without Nazis" announced it would gather at the same location shortly before the 6:30pm start of the 612 procession. All Points North's latest episode examines the legacy of Finland's dwindling war generation. Listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. The day concludes with the Independence Day Reception at the Presidential Palace, where invited guests celebrate with President Stubb and his spouse. Yle's live broadcast of the event begins at 6:15pm on Saturday. The Presidential Reception can be watched in the embedded player below. The gala remains Finland's most-watched annual television event.

Headline: The last of Finland's never-forgotten generation
Full_Text: Independence Day in Finland is a mostly sombre affair. Hietaniemi Cemetery in Helsinki, usually bordered by crowds on the nearby beach during the summer, takes on a far more solemn atmosphere in early December. Gravestones are freshly cleaned, memorials are tended, and officials gather to commemorate those who fought for Finland in the Winter War, Continuation War and Lapland War. The ones who survived the three conflicts make up Finland's revered but ever dwindling pool of war veterans — and every year that heroic generation seems to slip further away. Finnish President Alexander Stubb made the decision last year to not invite the veterans to the Independence Day gala — but instead to a separate, quieter event designed specifically for Finland's oldest surviving soldiers. Although a controversial decision at the time, Sakari Martimo of the Tammenlehvän Perinneliitto veterans' heritage organisation notes that the change reflects practical considerations. "These are 100-year-old people who have to travel even from the northern part of Finland," he told the podcast All Points North, adding that the new arrangement allows the president to devote his "full attention to the veterans for two whole hours". Around 20 veterans were able to attend the ceremony this year. By 2035, the last of Finland's wartime veterans will likely have passed away. All Points North's latest episode examines the legacy of Finland's dwindling war generation. Listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. Commemorative traditions for veterans and members of Lotta Svärd, a voluntary auxiliary paramilitary organisation for women during the wars, have adapted over time. Historian Olli Kleemola from the University of Turku tells APN that veterans were not always a prominent part of the Independence Day reception. "It is really only after the end of the Cold War," he said, pointing to President Mauno Koivisto's decision to invite veterans in 1989 on the 50th anniversary of the Winter War. During the Cold War, openly commemorating the wars risked irritating the Soviet Union, whose influence shaped much of Finnish political life. Only after the collapse of the Soviet Union did public appreciation of veterans expand, as retired servicemen had more time to publish books, participate in organisations and shape collective memory. With the wartime generation now more than a century old, much of their history is shifting from lived experience to recorded research. American historian and YouTuber Ian McCollum, who has worked with the Military Museum of Finland on a forthcoming book titled Forged in Snow, said Finland's experience remains a powerful example of national resistance. "I think especially compared to the United States, Finland has a really important firsthand experience of why it can be worth going to war," McCollum told the All Points North podcast. McCollum added that Finland's history of small arms reflects a small country that made the best with what it could acquire to defend itself. McCollum's new book details every single small arm manufactured and modified since Finland became independent in 1917. "Being willing to take that fight on is what kept Finland a sovereign country," he said. "There's a really important firsthand lesson in that."

Headline: Finland's war veterans get early Independence Day honours
Full_Text: Veterans and members of Lotta Svärd, a voluntary auxiliary paramilitary organisation for women, are celebrating Finnish independence on Tuesday at the Presidential Palace. It is taking place a few days ahead of the official holiday on Saturday 6 December. Tuesday's event brings together people of Finland's wartime generation, including veterans and Lotta Svärd members, hosted by President Alexander Stubb and his spouse Suzanne Innes-Stubb. The afternoon reception will also feature other members of the country's political leadership, with performances by the Guard's Band and singers from the National Opera. Just under 20 guests of honour are expected, with an average age exceeding 100. According to the President's Office, the daytime reception is designed to accommodate multiple guests and allow for unhurried conversations that take into account their advanced age and health. Every year, the President's Office announces a theme ahead of the official reception on 6 December. This year, the event will highlight the role of education and learning as cornerstones of Finnish society, according to Stubb's office. Yle will offer live coverage of Saturday's Independence Day gala on TV and its streaming platform Yle Areena. Edited at 15:50 on 2 December 2025 to include photos and video from the event.

Headline: Christmas season opens with first Advent Sunday
Full_Text: In churches across the country, congregations on Sunday are singing Hoosianna, the opening hymn of the Finnish hymnal. More than two centuries old, the hymn reflects the intertwined histories of Finland and Sweden. Turku's musical society is believed to have performed it for the first time in 1807. The word "hosanna," which appears in the New Testament, is the Greek form of an originally Hebrew cry for help addressed to a king or to God. Around 62 percent of Finland's population belongs to the Evangelical Lutheran Church. Watch Helsinki kick off the Christmas season with its traditional opening parade, one of Finland's largest festive events.

Headline: "You no longer have to be so serious" — gospel music sweeps Finnish congregations
Full_Text: Gospel music is growing in popularity. Over the past couple of years, Finnish congregations have established several gospel choirs, and this autumn Jyväskylä parish's new choir saw a surge in applications. So many people applied that the parish had to raise the participation cap from 50 to 120. Nationwide, the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland says that gospel's popularity is on the rise. Gospel is rhythmic spiritual music with roots in African-American culture. The word 'gospel' means 'good news.' As a Christian music genre, gospel is more energetic than classical choral music. A gospel choir is often accompanied by a band, and singers incorporate dance into their performances. Jyväskylä is not the only city where gospel is gaining ground. Teija Tuukkanen of the Church Council of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland said that several gospel choirs have been established in Finland over the past couple of years. The change reflects Finnish church music becoming more diverse. "You no longer have to be so serious — you can also embrace joy. The choir, for example, is allowed to dance in church," Tuukkanen explained. Helsinki, Kokkola, Tammisaari, Tampere and Kuopio now have gospel choirs. This autumn, new choirs have also started in Lappeenranta and Saarijärvi, in addition to Jyväskylä. Gospel has also attracted people who might not otherwise have been interested in joining a church choir, according to Tuukkanen. Nowadays, younger church music directors often have a background in popular rather than classical music, helping to fuel the trend. Tuukkanen also noted that improved language skills among congregants and church staff have made it easier to include English-language music in services. Jyväskylä parish's gospel choir performs songs in their original language, English.

Headline: Spotify's audiobook rollout in Finland takes authors by surprise
Full_Text: According to digital media expert and Yle's streaming services chief, Kari Haakana, audiobooks on Spotify may introduce the medium to new customers. "It may bring people who don't have audiobook subscriptions to listen to audiobooks," he said. On Tuesday, Spotify started offering audiobooks, joining competing platforms like BookBeat, Storytel, Nextory and Audible. Monthly subscription rates for audiobook services range from around 10 to more than 20 euros per month, depending on the amount of content offered and consumed. Nearly all of Finland's public libraries also offer free e-library services which include audiobooks, e-books and digital periodicals and newspapers. According to Spotify, a 12.99-euro premium monthly subscription includes access to around 300,000 audiobooks, along with the platform's broad selection of streamable music and podcasts. However, it remains to be seen how beneficial the development will be for authors, according to Haakana. "Consumers may win in the short term — there are lots of titles to choose from and prices are kept reasonable. But will that mean authors will benefit? I don't know," Haakana said. Yle spoke with authors in Finland who said that Spotify and their publishers made the audiobook streaming agreement without their participation. They include authors at publishing house Otava — Koko Hubara and Pajtim Statovci — and Gummerus author Juha Itkonen. They said they learned about their work being on Spotify on Tuesday, when the platform began offering them. According to Itkonen, Gummerus gave its writers an opportunity to decide whether they want their works to be on Spotify. On the other hand, Otava has already uploaded several audiobooks to the platform. Hubara told Yle that she learned about the Spotify news from a Helsingin Sanomat article on Tuesday. Hubara and Statovci said they were surprised Otava did not discuss the decision with its writers, noting that the publisher has organised discussions about legal matters or tax changes, for example. "The issue should have been communicated differently, for example by immediately inviting the authors to a joint discussion about the issue and giving them the opportunity to ask critical questions," Statovci told Yle by email. However, all three authors acknowledged that they agreed to giving the publishers the authority to decide how their work would be distributed when they signed their contracts. Hubara emphasised that her criticism is particularly directed to the publisher's communication about the matter. She also suggested that her publisher earns larger sums of money compared to the authors they take on. According to Statovci, authors understand they don't have much say about publishers' decisions about the distribution and pricing of books. Meanwhile, Itkonen emphasised that he does not want to "start a war" with publishers. He added that he understands that agreements between publishers and Spotify inherently involve a degree of business secrecy. "Nevertheless, it highlights that the writer is somehow in a weak position, in the dark and helpless. Decisions are made without us being heard," Itkonen said. Itkonen's publisher has argued that Spotify is a platform worth using. It has also noted that Spotify does not pay less than other audiobook services and that putting audiobooks there can help reach new audiences. Hubara said she felt it was unfair how her publisher was vague about the compensation model information. The publisher's email to her stated that Spotify uses a similar payment model as other listening-time based platforms. Itkonen said he thinks it is a positive development that payment for audiobook listens on Spotify are on a per-minute basis. A Spotify premium subscription at 12.99 euros per month offers customers 12 hours of audiobook listening per month. Customers can listen to more, but that comes at additional cost. People without Spotify subscriptions can also purchase individual audiobooks. According to the CEO of publishing house WSOY, Timo Julkunen, the company has been telling its authors about Spotify's plans to bring audiobooks to the Nordic market for the past couple of years. However, he said that due to the agreement it made with Spotify, the publisher was unable to tell the authors in advance about the actual starting date. "We try to be as open with our writers as possible. This was a legal matter," Julkunen said. Otava's sales chief, Nona Ratia, echoed that statement, saying that its agreement with Spotify only allowed the publisher to inform authors on Tuesday. Authors have for some time complained that the compensation they receive for audiobooks is too low. WSOY's Julkunen said he shares those concerns, adding that publishers are in the same boat. "I'd like to point out that many authors have received significant income from audiobook services," he said. Generally, the publishers think that Spotify will be a good addition to the Finnish audiobook market, a sentiment shared by Otava's sales chief Ratia. "We think it is a good thing that there are several players and competitors in the audiobook market. We believe that overall literature sales will grow," Ratia said.

Headline: Star conductor Salonen nominated for 3rd Grammy Award
Full_Text: Finnish conductor and composer Esa-Pekka Salonen could score his third Grammy Award in Los Angeles in February. The US Recording Academy announced its nominations late Friday, with Salonen nominated in the Best Orchestral Performance category. The nod comes for his recording of Igor Stravinsky’s Symphony in Three Movements with the San Francisco Symphony Orchestra. The album was recorded live in its home city in late 2023. That was just a few months before Salonen’s surprise announcement that he would leave the orchestra when his contract expired at the end of the 2024-25 season, the San Francisco Chronicle reports. He cited differences of opinion with the orchestra’s board about its future direction. Last year, during Salonen’s final season as music director, he and the orchestra picked up three Grammy nominations, one for their recording of Stravinsky’s "Firebird" and two for their world premiere recording of Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho’s opera Adriana Mater". The latter album won the Grammy for Best Opera Recording in February. It was recorded in the summer of 2023, just a few days after Saariaho’s death from cancer at the age of 70. She and Salonen, 67, were close friends for decades. In 1977, they were co-founders of the influential Korvat auki ("Ears Open") association of young composers. Although Salonen left the orchestra in June, the SFS still has plans to release more recordings by Salonen with the orchestra. He first led the ensemble in 2004. In September, the Orchestre de Paris appointed Salonen as principal conductor for a five-year contract beginning in 2027, while the Los Angeles Philharmonic appointed him as creative director, starting next year. Salonen has racked up a dozen US Recording Academy nominations. He picked up his first Grammy in 2009, when his recording with violinist Hilary Hahn and the Swedish Radio Symphony Orchestra won in the Best Instrumental Soloist(s) Performance (with orchestra) category. That same year, pianist Gloria Cheng won the award for Best Instrumental Soloist Performance (without Orchestra) for an album featuring works by Salonen and two others. Last year, Salonen was honoured alongside guitarist-producer Nile Rodgers with the 2024 Polar Music Prize in Stockholm, after conducting the 2023 Nobel Prize Concert there. A younger Finnish conductor was also up for an award at last February’s Grammy ceremony. Susanna Mälkki was nominated for Best Orchestral Performance for an album of Jean Sibelius pieces performed by the Helsinki Philharmonic Orchestra. The 68th Grammy Awards ceremony is scheduled for 1 February in Los Angeles.

Headline: Wednesday's papers: Finnair's foibles, lost in translation, and daycare haircuts
Full_Text: Domestic outlets, including Ilta-Sanomat, report on the latest developments regarding Finnair's laundry mishap, which forced the airline to cancel dozens of flights. Finnair will not compensate passengers for flights grounded by a laundry fiasco that left seat covers on eight Airbus A321s improperly washed and possibly less fire-resistant. The carrier argues that the cancellations fall under 'extraordinary circumstances' as defined by EU aviation regulations, grounds that exempt airlines from mandatory compensation. Passengers are reportedly less than pleased with that decision. All Points North recently looked into a turbulent year for Finnair. Listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. Finland is officially bilingual, with both Finnish and Swedish enjoying equal status under the law. In practice, though, public signs and official notices in Swedish are frequently misspelled, mistranslated or omitted altogether. Hufvudstadsbladet draws attention to three problematic mistranslations in Statistics Finland's communications in one week alone. Mistakes include confusing words like 'most' and 'least', inverting the intended meaning of official communications. The leading Swedish-language daily also noted that of the over 100 news releases the state agency has published on its website this year, only nine have been translated into Swedish. Helsingin Sanomat follows up its recent comparisons of Spanish and Finnish education with the discovery that some nurseries are offering an unexpected service: haircuts. Anni Holmström, a Finn living in Spain, was delighted when her two-year-old's hair was trimmed during the nursery day. The daycare salon visit took less than ten minutes and cost 20 euros. She calls the idea brilliant: parents save time, children stay calm in a familiar environment and everyone leaves looking a little neater. Finnish early-childhood officials were less enthused, though they said the idea sounded fun. The concept, they said, would be impossible to replicate in Finland, where strict rules govern what can happen in daycare settings. "In Finland, we tend to see more risks than opportunities, and we love our rules," mother-of-two Holmström told HS. "In Spain, the atmosphere is different. People are more relaxed, and not every regulation has to be followed to the letter."

Headline: Tuesday's papers: A seat at the table, a renter's market, and kids eat too
Full_Text: Finland has been working behind the scenes to advocate for Ukraine ahead of a planned Trump–Putin meeting in Budapest. But according to Kauppalehti, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is, for now at least, not expected to attend the meeting in Budapest, where US President Donald Trump plans to meet Russia's Vladimir Putin in an effort to bring an end to the war in Ukraine. Finland and key European countries are working behind the scenes to promote a just peace for Ukraine. This effort is being carried out within the so-called coalition of the willing, which includes 26 nations, as well as a smaller Ukraine-focused group, both of which Finland participates in under Stubb’s leadership, the business daily explained. In Helsinki and across the capital region, rents are falling at a pace not seen before, reports Helsingin Sanomat. The decline in rents, which began in the spring, has accelerated through late summer and early autumn. Now, tenants are being enticed with gift cards worth hundreds of euros and rent-free months, as an oversupply of rental flats floods the market. Corporate landlords are offering potential tenants a month — or even a full month — of free rent at the start of their lease, as well as gift cards to furniture and grocery stores. "Finns should be more willing to go out to eat with their kids," Carlos Henriques, the proprietor of Elm's in Helsinki, told Hufvudstadsbladet. Henriques, originally from Portugal, has lived in Finland for 14 years. His restaurant has piqued the Swedish-language daily's interest by offering babysitting services that have reportedly proven popular. He said that Finns' attitudes toward children in restaurants and public spaces differ sharply from those in southern Europe. "I come from a culture where children are part of everything," he said. "For us, it feels strange to think they wouldn't be included at dinner." Even so, Henriques observed that attitudes in Finland are gradually changing. People are slowly learning that neither fellow diners nor restaurant staff regard children as a burden.

Headline: Monday's papers: Banking privacy, from MoMA to Helsinki, and going to waste
Full_Text: The financial industry is worried about changes that would give tax officials broader rights to people's banking information. Business magazine Talouselämä explores a proposal put forward by the government that would grant Finland's Tax Administration broader powers to request information about taxpayers' finances. Finance Finland, an industry group, has sharply criticised the reform, arguing that it would open the door to extensive, large-scale data requests without the need to specify individual targets. Responding to the criticism, the finance ministry told the magazine that any information request made by the tax office must be justified and narrowly focused on data deemed essential for tax supervision. The proposal aims to support efforts to combat the grey economy, according to TE. The bill has now moved to parliament for consideration, with the law scheduled to take effect at the beginning of next year. Carson Chan, most recently curator of architecture and design at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York, has been appointed chief curator of the Architecture and Design Museum in Helsinki. His job will be to lead the curatorial team at the Finnish museum, which is slated to relocate to Helsinki's South Harbour waterfront in 2030. "The museum is a public institution of learning," Chan told Hufvudstadsbladet. "We do not engage in politics in the way politicians do, but we can take clear positions and shape how people think about issues such as the climate crisis," he said. "When it comes to climate change issues, we don't just need to reach people in their sixties, we need to engage the six-year-olds," Chan told the paper. Plastic recycling is not always as straightforward as people think, according to Maaseudun Tulevaisuus. Many people, without much thought, drop used plastic freezer bags into plastic recycling, but these actually belong in mixed waste, according to the agricultural paper. Only plastics that have served as packaging can be recycled as plastic waste, while general plastic items cannot. For example, the small plastic bags used for fruit and vegetables in stores are recyclable because they function as packaging, but biodegradable plastic bags, on the other hand, are not.

Headline: STT: Spanish painting missing for centuries found in Finnish gallery
Full_Text: A painting by the Spanish Baroque artist Antonio del Castillo y Saavedra (1616–1668), which was thought to have been lost for hundreds of years, has been discovered on display at the Villa Gyllenberg Art Museum in Helsinki. The artwork, entitled Saint Peter Martyr, was painted sometime between 1650 and 1655 as part of a series depicting saints that originally belonged to the Dominican monastery of San Pablo in Córdoba, southern Spain. The painting has been missing since around 1830, when the Spanish state sold the monastery's properties and confiscated its assets. The San Pablo series, which includes 10 paintings in total, was broken up and was believed for centuries to have been lost. According to Finnish news agency STT, Villa Gyllenberg's Chief Curator Lotta Nylund was on holiday in Andalusia last year when she spotted a plaque at the Fine Arts Museum in the city of Córdoba which read: "Saint Peter Martyr – location unknown". "I think I know where this lost work is located," Nylund tells STT of her thoughts at the time. "When I got home, I compared the measurements of the works and read all the research literature, and it started to look more and more likely that the painting at Villa Gyllenberg is actually one of the missing parts of the Córdoba series." Further research confirmed her suspicions, and collaboration between the two museums led to Castillo expert José María Palencia Cerezo travelling to Helsinki to confirm the work was part of the San Pablo series. Finnish art collector Ane Gyllenberg purchased the painting from a gallery in London in 1934. An exhibition of Gyllenberg's collection — including the once-lost Saint Peter Martyr — will open at Villa Gyllenberg on 15 October.

Headline: "People don't have babies to make taxpayers" — Finland's childfree defend choices amid shrinking population debate
Full_Text: As news of shrinking municipalities, an ageing population and record-low birthrates continue to dominate Finnish headlines, a growing share of people in Finland are choosing to be childfree. The proportion of childless adults in Finland is among the highest in Europe and OECD countries, based on data from the Family Federation of Finland. Around one in five women and more than one in four men born in the late 1960s and early 1980s — now aged 45–55 — are childless and will likely remain so due to their age. According to a 2025 government report, the country's birth rate has fallen more rapidly than expected during this decade, primarily because of a decrease in first births. But amid public and political debate on the "population crisis," childfree people in Finland argue that the discussion too often shifts to concerns about an ageing population and who will prop up the welfare system. Soile Rajamäki, chairperson of the Finnish Childfree Association (Vapaaehtoiset Lapsettomat in Finnish), says this framing is problematic and calls for a complete rethink. "What is missing in this discussion is the fact that the Finnish pension system is a man-made structure — it's not a force of nature that is inescapable. This structure has clearly outlived its usefulness, and we need a new, better one that adapts to changing times, where many people simply don't want to have children," she says. Rajamäki added that supporting the welfare system is the last thing on people's minds when deciding to have children. "I doubt if there are really any parents who have children because the country needs new taxpayers," Rajamäki says. According to Rajamäki, with the severe cuts in the social welfare system, including mental health care, education, and childcare, "there's no guarantee that even the children born today are going to be healthy and productive members of society". New estimates by the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health show that government social security cuts will push over 30,000 children below the poverty line, raising child poverty by three percentage points. Rajamäki, who joined the association of voluntarily childfree people in 2016, said the group aims to provide peer support for those who make this valid lifestyle choice but are often made to feel like outliers. "I grew up in a small, conservative and religious town where it was clear what a girl's life was supposed to be. But I always knew that was not my path. In my 20s, I made a firm decision not to have children, though I initially felt alone and alienated until I found others like me and this organisation," she says. Among the group's members, the reasons for choosing to be childfree are varied, ranging from a desire for an independent life to concerns about the environment, the future, and uncertainty about what lies ahead. She says the freedom to make that choice is especially important for women's rights. "For some people, it's not even an active decision. It's just who they are. But I would say, most child-free people want to have a nice, quiet and easy life and the unrestricted ability to pursue the life they want," Rajamäki says. While the association organises social activities like picnics, cultural visits, and hiking for its members, it also focuses on advocacy issues. "Especially in the current climate, we've spoken out against a government proposal to ban sterilisations and vasectomies in public healthcare. This kind of policy is a slippery slope and a gateway to even more dangerous decisions on individuals' reproductive and sexual rights," she adds. Back in the late 1970s and early '80s, only about 4–10 percent of Finnish 20–35-year-olds without kids thought that having zero children was the ideal. But among those born in 1985–1994, the share has already climbed to around 20 percent, according to findings from surveys conducted between 2007 and 2018 by the Family Federation of Finland. Kateryna Golovina, a postdoctoral researcher at the Federation, says the reasons for this are a combination of objective uncertainties — such as unfinished studies, unstable job situations — and "perceived uncertainty" about the global situation, climate and their own ability to provide for a child. She says in the past, having children was not really a choice, but something everyone just did because of social expectations. But now people actively have to make that decision. "In the last few decades, expectations around raising children have increased greatly, be it financially or in terms of time and energy — there's this idea of intensive parenthood. In our research, we found that many who chose to stay childfree said they didn’t feel suitable for parenting. For them, it was simply not the right path," she says. Golovina adds that another key factor is the reluctance to change one's current lifestyle. Many people want to travel, build a career, or pursue other activities they see as incompatible with childbearing, which often leads them to postpone parenthood. One reason for Finland's high rate of childlessness, according to the statistics from the Family Federation of Finland, is that people are delaying parenthood, meaning some reach the end of their fertile years without having a first child. For some, like Raquel Leesmaa Becerra, uncertainty in Finland's volatile job market has led them to postpone or forgo having children. Becerra, 32, from Mexico, says she always expected to have children, which drew her to Finland, known for its family-friendly environment and safety. However, she lost her permanent job in 2024 when the company shut down, and she has been unemployed for around 14 months. She even received letters from immigration authority Migri about the possibility of deportation until she switched her residence permit from employment-based to family ties. "How can I feel ready to become a mother, considering how uncertain my future is here? The family and children I hope to have deserve so much more than the bare minimum," she says. According to Becerra, she wouldn't want to parent solely relying on state support and government handouts, especially with the increasing number of cuts in the social sector. "If I reach 38 and don’t have kids, it won't happen for me. I still have a few years to figure it out, but if the situation isn't changing, I am not sure anymore," Becerra explains. According to her, integration of foreigners goes beyond just discussions of learning the language, but also facilitating a stable environment where they feel secure starting a family. "I would think it’s more of a gain for Finland to help people who have grounds to stay in the country and make it easier for them. Integration plans are not working anymore if people can't imagine their future they desire for themselves," she adds. Finland has a relatively generous family policy, which includes paid parental leave, a universal child allowance for every child under 17, and a home care allowance for children under three who are not in daycare. However, the promise of state support alone is not enough to convince people to have children, says Karolina Mackiewicz, 42, from Poland, who has voluntarily chosen a childfree life, adding that raising a child requires much more than financial incentives. "As a foreigner in Finland, I see my peers struggling with raising kids without a community, without a 'village.' Institutions or the state don't give you what your closest family gives you. I see families with children, and I never feel like I'm missing out," she says. Mackiewicz adds that there is no single reason for her decision to remain childfree — it simply came naturally to her. "When I decided 15 years ago, people kept saying, 'You'll change your mind, you'll get pregnant.' But I never felt that calling, and sometimes, it felt odd to even have to defend my decision." According to Mackiewicz, although she drifted apart from many friends who became absorbed in playdates and family events as the years went by, she has built a life that is independent, fulfilling, and exactly as she imagined. "My partner and I have been together for 13 years. From the start, it was clear that I didn't want children, which made things easier, and there was no pressure from my partner. We’re happy, spending our free time and disposable income on travel. Sometimes, I even feel guilty for having it too easy in life." According to Kateryna Golovina from the Family Federation of Finland, while Finland's family-friendly policies help support parents and likely prevent the birth rate from falling even further, ultimately, no policy can force people to have children. In fact, paying women to have more babies doesn't work because it fails to address the underlying issues, like work pressures. "Raising maternal benefits or allowances a bit wouldn't suddenly make people want kids, and no one can be coerced into doing so," she says. Support should go to those who want children, but there's also a large group of people who are hesitant, undecided, or ambivalent, according to Golovina. "For that group, it may help to show that parenthood is not only about crying children and constant stress. It is demanding and difficult, but it also brings many rewards. Social media plays a role in shaping perceptions, so understanding how young people imagine parenthood is important." However, she said, ultimately, it's important to support people in their choices. "If people want to be childfree, that’s their choice, and we respect it. If they want children, we should support them. And for those who are hesitant or unsure, we can show what parenthood could be like so they can make an informed decision," she says. Headline: APN Podcast: Young migrants bring their stories to the stage
Full_Text: What's it like to arrive in Finland as a minor with no parents? In this episode of All Points North, we explore a youth theatre production where young people from Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria, Kurdistan and Ukraine turn their challenging journeys into stories of resilience and belonging. The show also touches on bigger migration issues in Finland, like the uncertain futures of these young performers who arrived here as unaccompanied minors. Listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. "In this society, we often talk about integration as a problem-oriented discussion, but here it's also our source of power — plurality — that everybody is so different and they come from different cultures," Jussi Lehtonen, head of communities and engagement at the Finnish National Theatre, told APN. Performers like Rozkin, Ada and Rizz bring their own stories to the stage, giving us a glimpse into what it's like to adapt and settle in a new country, ultimately finding their place in Finnish society. Headline: Finland's Moomin series gets international Emmy nod
Full_Text: The fourth season of Finland's animated TV series Moominvalley (Moominlaakso in Finnish) has been nominated for an international Emmy Award by the International Academy of Television Arts and Sciences. In its announcement, the academy revealed 64 nominees from 26 countries across 16 categories. This year marked the second time that Moominvalley has received an Emmy nod — it was first nominated in 2020. Moominvalley is the latest in a number of animated series about Finland's beloved Moomin family and cast of peculiar characters. The series is jointly produced by the Finnish firm Gusty Animations and Yle, the Finnish Broadcasting Company. In the Finnish version, Moominvalley's characters are voiced by actors including Joonas Nordman, Satu Silvio and Olavi Uusivirta. When the series began in 2019, it was reportedly Finland's most expensive TV production. Moominvalley can be seen on Yle's multimedia streaming platform Areena. Finnish actor Maria Sid was also nominated for an international Emmy, in the best female actor category, for her work in the Swedish series Pressure Point (Smärtpunkten in Swedish). The series is about a playwright and producer who decided to develop a play featuring inmates at a high-security prison — but their aim to help rehabilitate their imprisoned actors doesn't go as planned. This year's Emmy gala is scheduled to be held in New York City on Monday, 24 November.

Headline: Finnish woman's Lego-built wedding dress goes on display in Denmark
Full_Text: Satu Aaltonen, a Lego enthusiast from the west coast Finnish city of Vaasa, has been invited to display her latest creation at the Masterpiece Gallery exhibition in Denmark. The gallery invites 15-17 contributors every year to showcase their brick-built masterpieces at the venue in Billund, the city where Lego's founder Ole Kirk Kristiansen started his toy-making business in 1932. Aaltonen is only the second Finn in history — and the first Finnish woman — to receive an invitation to the exhibition, which "celebrates creativity and shows that the possibilities with Lego bricks are endless when you use your imagination", according to the company's website. Aaltonen’s creation is a wearable wedding dress, called the Bride of the Frozen Crown, and it was built from thousands of Lego bricks. "I wanted to create something out of Lego that has not been seen before. For me, building is both art and play, but also a meditative counterbalance to my everyday computer work," Aaltonen told Yle. The dress is fully wearable and Aaltonen did not use any glue when building it. "When moving in the dress, it makes a sound like walking on ice. The Lego pieces rattle against each other," she said. The dress is designed so that one side can be opened and closed, but Aaltonen admitted that she wouldn't dare to sit down while wearing it. "But you only need to walk to the altar and dance a little at the wedding party," she said with a smile. Eero Okkonen is the only other Finn to have been invited to display their works at the Masterpiece Gallery. Okkonen is also chair of the Finnish Lego enthusiasts’ association Palikkatakomo, and he considers Aaltonen's invitation to be a significant recognition of her creativity. "It’s one of the greatest honors you can receive for your hobby. Over the course of its history, only about a hundred enthusiasts have been invited to the exhibition in Denmark," he said. The dress going on display in Billund is one of a series of six that Aaltonen is currently building. "The greatest compliment is when people are surprised to discover that the dresses are made of Lego bricks. I want to inspire wonder in viewers and show that creativity has no limits," Aaltonen said.

Headline: Jury unanimous on winning design of Helsinki's new harbourside museum
Full_Text: The design of Helsinki's new Museum of Architecture and Design, set to be located in the capital's South Harbour district, has been chosen following an anonymous competition. The winning design, named "Kumma" (which can mean "peculiar" or "curious" in Finnish), was submitted by the Finnish architectural firm JKMM Architects. The company is renowned for having also designed the Amos Rex art museum building, the capital's Dance House, as well as a new extension to Finland's National Museum. "Kumma respects the cultural landscape of the South Harbour, preserving important views from Tähtitorninvuori towards the Market Square and Katajanokka, while establishing a clearly recognisable new landmark," the company said in a press release. The budget for the construction of the new museum is estimated to be about 105 million euros, with work expected to begin by the end of 2027 and doors set to open to the public in 2030. The museum will be located at the same site as the previously-planned Guggenheim art museum, which was voted down by the Helsinki city council in 2016. JKMM's illustrations show the impact Kumma will have on Helsinki's skyline: The open and anonymous design competition was launched in 2024, and a total of 624 entries were submitted from across the world, five of which advanced to the final stage. Samuli Miettinen, principal designer at JKMM, told Yle that he hopes the museum will become a landmark location. "Maybe, in the future, hockey world championships will be celebrated in front of Kumma Square instead of at Havis Amanda," Miettinen said.

Headline: Sarah Dzafce crowned Miss Finland 2025
Full_Text: Sarah Dzafce has been named Miss Finland 2025, according Iltalehti. Dzafce credited her victory to strong family support. With a father from Kosovo and a mother from Finland, she said her mixed heritage has made it easier to connect with people from varied backgrounds. The first runner-up was Tara Lehtonen, with Julianna Kauhaniemi taking the second runner-up position. The competition was staged at the Hype arena in Espoo on Saturday. Finland has a long history of beauty contests. Archived pageants from 1933 to 1978 are available on Yle's Areena streaming service.

Headline: Children wrote to Moominvalley, and Tove Jansson replied
Full_Text: Moominland, near Sweden. One letter addressed like this made its way to Finland all the way from Australia. Somewhat miraculously, letters sent to Tove Jansson (1914–2001) almost always found their way to the Finnish author and illustrator. Jansson received more than 1,500 letters and postcards from around the world every year, and this volume of mail kept arriving for decades. Many were addressed to characters from her Moomin books, sometimes simply to Moominvalley. Postal workers across the globe must have known that the Moomins and Jansson herself were linked to Finland. In her new book, Tove Jansson ja maailman lapset ("Tove Jansson and the Children of the World"), art historian Tuula Karjalainen noted that Jansson felt compelled to reply to every letter. Many of Jansson's letters are preserved at the Åbo Akademi library. Tracking down the original recipients required some detective work. They were scattered across the globe. Many handed over the letters for Karjalainen's use, though some were more cautious, given the sometimes deeply personal nature of their correspondence. Many of the children's letters conveyed a sense of loneliness and alienation. The young letter writers often confided problems with family or friends. In 1988, a girl from Espoo wrote: "I have very few friends, and they all live far away. I don't like school. I don't want to go, but tomorrow is Monday, and I have to. Our classroom has a mailbox. During the week, letters are placed inside, and on Fridays the box is opened and the letters are distributed. I have never received a single letter from the mailbox." On loneliness, Jansson once replied: "It took me 30 years before I began to enjoy it [loneliness], and many more before it became a necessity, and many more still before I realised that my solitude is a rare luxury — so long as it is voluntary, and I can interrupt it at any time. Of true loneliness I know nothing, not yet. In fact, almost nothing at all." "Tove was a remote therapist," Karjalainen said, adding that Jansson understood that children needed a sympathetic ear. "What surprised me most was how openly Tove wrote about herself and her life." Most correspondents, however, wanted to learn more about the inhabitants of Moominvalley, with the Groke attracting the most curiosity. Many letters asked Jansson about her favourite character or who she would most like to be. To Karjalainen's surprise, in one reply, Jansson said she would like to be a Hattifattener. Hattifatteners are famously silent, anonymous and devoid of compassion, moving in groups without obligations. "They're quite far from Tove," Karjalainen said. Jansson continued to receive letters from children until her death, many pleading for new Moomin books. Jansson wrote her final Moomin book, Moominvalley in November, in 1970. Darker in tone than her earlier works, it speaks more to adult readers. Jansson, beloved worldwide for her Moomin stories, was also a celebrated painter, illustrator and cartoonist who also wrote novels and short stories for adults. As a Swedish-speaking Finn, she wrote in Swedish, but her tales have wandered into more than 50 languages, carrying Moominvalley far beyond Finland's borders. That includes a controversial exhibition in New York this summer, marking the 80th anniversary of the publication of the first Moomin tale in 1945.

Headline: Friday's papers: Finnish ambassador to the US, union wealth and repurposed power plant
Full_Text: Tabloid Iltalehti sat down for an interview with Finland's ambassador to the United States, Leena-Kaisa Mikkola. "For now we are at the table — and that is good — but whether we will be in the future is another matter," she told IL. Two days before President Alexander Stubb met Donald Trump and other European leaders in Washington, Finland's ambassador to the United States, Mikkola was preparing her staff for what she described as a historic moment. Mikkola said Stubb's visible role and his good personal relations with Trump have increased interest in Finland in Washington. She stressed that it was not just about visibility — Stubb was being listened to and his views respected. While US media has dubbed Stubb a "Trump whisperer", Mikkola cautioned against assuming Finland would always have such access. She confirmed that Finland's image in the US capital is strong. "Finland is seen as a reliable Northern European partner with a lot to offer, whether it is expertise on Russia or on technology." Nato membership, she added, has further strengthened ties with the White House and US defence institutions. Yle News reporter Matthew Schilke covered Finnish President Alexander Stubb's attendance at the meeting in Washington in the video below. Mikkola said she was not surprised to see Finland's president at the White House table, citing Stubb's established relationship with Trump and his role among European leaders. "After 30 years in the service, few things surprise me," she noted. She added that Finland, as Russia's neighbour, benefited from being close to where such decisions are made. "It is wonderful if we can get closer to the tables where these things are discussed." She described Stubb's presence in Washington as personally gratifying. "Of course it feels good for a Finnish diplomat." Finland's ten wealthiest trade unions hold close to three billion euros in assets, according to business daily Kauppalehti. Returns on investments have become a crucial source of funding, particularly during periods of industrial action and strikes. The Industrial Union is among the richest, with nearly 900 million euros in equity. But its operations ran at a loss in 2024, as strike compensation drove up costs. Investment income of 39 million euros was not enough to cover the shortfall. At the end of last year, public and welfare sector trade union JHL had an equity of 500 million euros, while service sector union Pam was worth 460 million euros. The Finnish Construction Trade Union held around 318 million euros worth of assets. Last spring, All Points North covered how the government's plan to eliminate certain tax deductions would impact unions. Listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. The Paperworkers' Union and white-collar union Pro were among the trade organisations posting deficits last year. Pro lost around one million euros on a failed hotel investment, while the paper union is weighing the sale of forest and land holdings in Loviisa. A significant share of union wealth is tied to the rental housing company Kojamo, part-owned by several unions. The firm, founded in the 1960s to ease Finland's housing shortage, has since become a key generator of dividend income. Helsingin Sanomat wrote that a rare property designed by renowned Finnish architect Eliel Saarinen has gone on sale in Helsinki's Meilahti district. Saarinen, one of Finland's most renowned architects, designed many of Helsinki's landmark buildings including the Central Railway Station and National Museum of Finland. The building for sale, originally a power plant inaugurated in 1915, has been converted into a detached home. What used to be the power plant's a transformer tower, has now been renovated into a small apartment with alcoves, a living room and terraces. The property remained in use as an energy facility until the 1950s, before serving as a workshop for the city's energy company. Helsinki put the site up for sale in 2012, after which extensive renovations began. The 200-square-metre home includes several unusual features reflecting its industrial past, such as a sauna and washroom built into an upper loft. Headline: Finland recaptures Air Guitar World title after 25-year hiatus
Full_Text: Aapo "The Angus" Rautio, 25, from Oulu, was crowned the air guitar world champion on Saturday evening in his home city. Rautio's victory means that the World Air Guitar title has now returned to the event’s host country, Finland, for the first time since 2000. This year, the World Air Guitar Championships also attracted an exceptional amount of interest from foreign media, making headlines as far afield as Australia and the United States. This is the local air guitarist's first championship win, but by no means his first time participating in the competition. Rautio first competed in the event when he was just 10 years old – that is, 15 years ago. Yle interviewed Rautio when he participated in the games for the first time over a decade ago: He won the world championship on his seventh attempt, after making it into the finals five times. Rautio narrowly edged out Yuta "Sudo-chan" Sudo of Japan for the gold medal, with Apolline "Lady Attila" Andreys of France coming in third. This year’s other competitors came from the Netherlands, Belgium, Great Britain, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Germany, Taiwan, New Zealand and the United States. "I knew from the beginning of the week that I really didn't want to take the competition too seriously," he told Yle. "I really just wanted to have fun." For him, the most important thing is not the contest itself, but the community that surrounds it. "We have a global network that’s like a family to me. These people aren’t just friends to me, they’re my sisters and brothers. And this family grows every year," he said.

Headline: Thursday's papers: School burka debate, Finnish food in Russia and Finns in Alaska
Full_Text: A group of Finns Party MPs, buoyed by fresh momentum, have issued a joint statement demanding that Education Minister Anders Adlercreutz (SPP) take action to ban Islamic face coverings in schools, reports Hufvudstadsbladet. This development follows a social media post on Wednesday by Sanni Grahn-Laasonen (NCP), Finland's Minister for Social Security, in which she voiced her opposition to the wearing of burqas and niqabs in schools. In a written response to HBL, Adlercreutz dismissed the idea of a headscarf ban as a political stunt. He said a ban would be a disproportionate measure, which risks hurting the people it aims to protect: young girls. "Marginalisation increases the risk of radicalisation. That is why it is important to maintain an open and inclusive society where everyone feels welcome," he told the Swedish-language daily. Why are Finnish food products still appearing on Russian shelves? The availability of Finnish sweets and alcoholic beverages contradicts claims by most Finnish companies that they have stopped exporting goods to Russia. According to Kauppalehti, Finnish products are reaching Russia through indirect routes via Estonia. The country is home to numerous transport and logistics companies that have continued exporting to Russia since the war in Ukraine began, with Finnish goods appearing on their export lists. "We do not condone our products being exported to Russia, but we've found it very difficult, if not impossible, to stop it, despite our efforts," a Fazer spokesperson told the business daily. On Friday, US President Donald Trump is set to discuss the war in Ukraine with Russian leader Vladimir Putin at a military base in Anchorage known as the Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. Finnish media is often keen to highlight a Finnish connection to world events, and has also done so in the case of this meeting, albeit tenuously. In this instance, Ilta-Sanomat reports that Werner Ohls, born in Turku in 1892, and his wife Ida, born in Vaasa in 1893, were among the first homesteaders in the area that is now the military base. The couple first arrived in Alaska during the gold rush in the early 1900s, later establishing a dairy farm that had 24 cows at its peak. Eventually, the US governemnt purchased the Ohls' 65-acre farm to make way for the base, according to IS.

Headline: Minister: "Burkas and niqabs are not suitable for school"
Full_Text: Finland's Minister of Social Security, Sanni Grahn-Laasonen (NCP), has spoken out on social media against the wearing of burkas and niqabs in schools. Posting on X, she said face coverings do not belong in schools. "Burkas and niqabs — scarves and veils covering the face — are not suitable for school. Children should be allowed to be children and live freely in Finnish society," the minister wrote. She described the issue as one of equality, children's rights and safety, and also addressed the broader use of headscarves, calling it "a difficult question of religious freedom." Burkas and niqabs are worn in some Islamic communities for religious and cultural reasons. "We have to have the courage to talk about how we protect women from oppressive religious cultures and work to ensure that no one in Finland has to cover their face," Grahn-Laasonen stated. Last month, Finance Minister Riikka Purra (Finns) called for a total ban on burkas, niqabs and headscarves, especially in schools. This followed a proposal, put forward by 15 Finns Party members last year, calling for a complete ban on face coverings in public places. The move would effectively mean a ban on the wearing in public of the burka — a traditional garment worn by some Muslim women that covers the face and body — as well as the niqab, a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. Reacting to Purra's comments, Education Minister Anders Adlercreutz (SPP) told Helsingin Sanomat that while face-coverings can be taken up in schools from a safety and identification perspective, he does not support legislative measures on the matter.

Headline: From Gothic Modern to Little My — Finnish art takes on the world
Full_Text: Global interest in Finnish art is reaching an unprecedentedly high level, with major exhibitions taking place across the world this year. The exhibitions feature a wide range of Finnish art offerings — from beloved classics to contemporary favourites, and from Gothic Modern to the Moomins. "Finnish art is on the rise internationally," Frame CEO Juha Huuskonen told Yle. Huuskonen's company, Frame Contemporary Art Finland, specialises in promoting the status and export of Finnish contemporary art worldwide. "Over the past 20 years, Finnish contemporary art has become more prominent abroad than ever before," he noted. "At the same time, these artists help to raise Finland's image and reputation as a country of culture." Anna-Maria von Bonsdorff, director of Ateneum Art Museum in downtown Helsinki, agrees with Huuskonen that Finnish art is becoming more popular than ever before. "We have worked hard to ensure that the works of Finnish artists gain visibility abroad. This is not a coincidence," she said. An exhibition of works by Finnish modernist painter Helene Schjerfbeck (1862–1946) opens at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York on 5 December. The event has been described as "historic", as it marks the first time a Finnish artist has had their own dedicated exhibition at one of the world's most prestigious art museums. "In the world of museums and from a cultural perspective, it is the number one museum in the world. That is why Schjerfbeck's exhibition at The Met is the most important art event of the year," Ateneum director Anna-Maria von Bonsdorff noted. The exhibition includes approximately 60 works in total, spanning Schjerfbeck's entire career from her early landscapes to her late-life self-portraits. Ateneum Art Museum loans hundreds of paintings by Finnish artists to various exhibitions every year, and von Bonsdorff tells Yle that the number has increased steadily over recent years. In November, the Petit Palais museum in Paris will be filled with works by Finnish painter Pekka Halonen (1865-1933), renowned in particular for his depictions of nature landscapes. "This is a topical issue in French culture right now and one that they are interested in," von Bonsdorff said. Halonen lived in Paris in the 1890s, studying art under famous painters including Paul Gauguin (1848-1903). "Pekka Halonen was a pioneer for other Finnish artists. He would certainly have been happy if he had known that an exhibition of his work would be held in Paris," von Bonsdorff said. Aside from loaning Finnish works of art to international museums, Ateneum also seeks to share exhibitions it has put together. For example, Ateneum's 'Gothic Modern' exhibition — featuring European medieval and Northern Renaissance art which ran from October 2024 to January 2025 — was also on display in Oslo and will soon open at the Albertina Museum in Vienna. The themes of the Gothic Modern exhibition include death and rituals, but also sexuality and enlightenment. Hugo Simberg (1873-1917) and Akseli Gallen-Kallela (1865-1931) are among the Finnish artists on display at the Albertina. The Moomins and the wider artworks of their creator Tove Jansson (1914-2001), have captured the attention of audiences from Japan to the United States. The Brooklyn Public Library in New York, for example, has an extensive Moomin exhibition. The Moomin exhibition made headlines recently when the library dropped the Stinky character after one of the institution's supporters raised concerns that it might be perceived as racist. Heli Harni, curator of the Helsinki Art Museum HAM, meanwhile told Yle that she witnessed at first hand the Japanese love for the Moomins at the opening of an exhibition of Jansson's works in Tokyo in July. "Everyone from babies to grandfathers in Japan is interested in the Moomins, and the exhibition has received a lot of attention," Harni said, adding that exhibitions such as this one help to build Finland's image abroad. In addition to the Moomins, the exhibition also features Tove Jansson's paintings as well as other personal items which tell the story of her life. The Jansson exhibition will also travel to other Japanese cities after Tokyo. Aside from the Moomins, Japanese people are also impressed by Finnish design. A large-scale solo exhibition by Tapio Wirkkala (1915–1985) is currently on display in Japan for the first time, retrospectively celebrating the artist's 110th birthday. Wirkkala is a renowned designer and sculptor, known in particular for his work with glass, silver and plywood. An exhibition of Finnish photographer Joel Karppanen's images from the Spanish holiday resort of Fuengirola — a popular destination for Finnish tourists — is currently open at the Cultural Institute of Madrid in Spain. Karppanen's collection — entitled 'Land of Dreams' — features some of the thousands of Finnish people who have fled the cold of their home country for the sunshine of southern Spain. According to Frame CEO Juha Huuskonen, young Finnish artists have more confidence in themselves than ever before as they dare to show their works to the world. He cites contemporary artists such as Eija-Liisa Ahtila and Jenna Sutela as examples of Finland's batch of brave young pioneers. Huuskonen noted, however, that a lot of hard work goes into securing exhibitions for Finnish artists outside of Finland. He said it requires extensive networking efforts by the artists themselves as well as cooperation between many different organisations. "We must work hard to open international channels," Huuskonen said. "It is important that we are able to renew ourselves and build something new, and not just remain as memories of the golden age of art."

Headline: Three elves cycle from Germany to Santa's village
Full_Text: Three postal workers set off on Saturday on a nearly 3,000-kilometre bike ride from Germany to Santa Claus Village in Rovaniemi, reports German news agency dpa. The cyclists are travelling north to deliver letters and Christmas wish lists addressed to Santa Claus from St. Nikolaus in Saarland state. Their journey, which will take them through Germany, Denmark, and Sweden, is expected to last three weeks. The group is part of the German postal service's volunteer team responsible for replying to children's letters from around the world sent to the St. Nikolaus post office. The village of St. Nikolaus is one of seven places in Germany with Christmas-themed names. All of these receive letters addressed either to Santa Claus or to Saint Nicholas, a key figure in German Christmas traditions. Each year, more than 30,000 letters arrive. This year, Saint Nicholas entrusted the cyclists with his own wish list, hoping to receive a reply from Santa Claus in Finland.

Headline: Flags fly for Moomin creator on Saturday
Full_Text: All across Finland on Saturday, flags are fluttering in celebration of author and artist Tove Jansson (1914-2001) and of Finnish art itself. Jansson, beloved worldwide for her Moomin stories, was also a celebrated painter, illustrator and cartoonist. As a Swedish-speaking Finn, she wrote in Swedish, but her tales have wandered into more than 50 languages, carrying Moominvalley far beyond Finland's borders. She published the first Moomin book, The Moomins and the Great Flood, just after the Second World War in 1945. Since 2020, the Ministry of the Interior has encouraged flag-raising on Jansson's birthday as a salute to Finnish art and creativity. Jansson's whimsical Moomin characters made headlines last week when a figure was removed from a major exhibition at the Brooklyn Public Library in New York, after a supporter of the institution raised concerns that it could be perceived as racist. The Brooklyn exhibition, the first in the United States to focus on Tove Jansson and the Moomins, has proven popular — especially among younger audiences. The New York Times noted that the Moomins' rise in popularity in the US is comparable to the cultural impact of Peanuts' Snoopy.

Headline: Flow Festival faces boycott calls over Israel links
Full_Text: Flow Festival, which opens in Helsinki on Friday, is facing unprecedented calls for a boycott over alleged links to Israel through its US majority owner, investment firm KKR, and some sponsors. The activist group Flow Strike says these ties make the event complicit in Israel's actions in Gaza, urging organisers to cut all Israeli connections or risk losing the festival's city permits. Flow was sold to UK-based Superstruct in 2018, which was itself acquired by KKR last year. KKR has global investments, including some in Israel, but these are relatively small, according to Finnish media. Sponsors such as Heineken and Google also operate in Israel. Flow's artistic director Tuomas Kallio has described the idea that the festival is directly linked to "apartheid and genocide" as "at best artificial," adding that almost every major player in the music industry has some connection to Israel. Several artists have voiced discomfort about performing, with some planning to donate their fees to Palestinian causes. Members of the band Ruusut said they will use their Saturday set to call for Finland to recognise Palestine and halt arms sales to Israel. The boycott campaign mirrors similar moves across Europe against cultural events with perceived Israeli ties.

Headline: Helsinki plans to bring back popular 'summer streets' next year
Full_Text: The City of Helsinki's "Summer Streets" initiative in Kallio, which transformed urban streets into more pedestrian-friendly zones, is set to return next year. City officials said that while most feedback from residents has focused on challenges like limited parking and changes to traffic flow, the overall response has been positive. "Helsinki residents have been very pleased. There have even been requests to bring summer streets to other parts of the city," said project engineer Pirita Ilmonen from the City of Helsinki. Yle News reporter Matthew Schilke asked locals what they thought about the summer pilot project. The street design was developed in collaboration with local residents and businesses. As part of the plan, parking spaces were replaced with plants, furniture, and light structures that can be easily removed for winter. New seating was added on Porthaninkatu, with plants and furniture along Fleminginkatu and near Karhupuisto park. An event stage opened by Kallio Library, and upgrades were made to squares around Kallio Church, Torkkelinaukio, Ympyrätalo, and Kolmas linja. "The plan is to recreate the summer streets in a similar form next year, but that will be confirmed in the fall." According to Ilmonen, no major changes are expected for next year, but lessons will be learned from this summer. "The summer shows what works and what may need to be adjusted." The project cost the City of Helsinki about 1.5 million euros.

Headline: Tuesday's papers: Stubb-Trump call, ministers at music fests and saving videogames
Full_Text: Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke on the phone with US President Donald Trump on Monday. Stubb shared the news on the social media platform X, reported Helsingin Sanomat. The conversation touched on, among other topics, Russia’s war of aggression. "President Trump’s deadline for a ceasefire is approaching. Finland supports all efforts towards an immediate ceasefire," Stubb wrote. According to Stubb, the conversation also continued on the topic of icebreakers as a part of security and cooperation among allies. Recently, President Stubb told Defence Forces' Ruotuväki magazine that he speaks weekly with the US President, aiming to strengthen Finland's role in the Ukrainian peace process and clarify the conditions for peace. A video from the Ruisrock festival showing politicians in high spirits made headlines, sparking public discussion over the costly gifts they receive. Iltalehti reported that 23 MPs — including Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) and four ministers — attended an invitation-only City of Turku event before Ruisrock and enjoyed the festival in early July, with most bringing guests. A video from the festival featuring Minister of Climate and the Environment Sari Multala (NCP) and PM Orpo speaking with rap duo JVG has since generated widespread buzz online. In it, artist Ville Galle remarks that the group is "totally drunk," to which a visibly tipsy Multala responds affirmatively. Multala declined to comment to IL about the matter. According to the City of Turku, ministers Orpo and Multala received invitations to Ruisrock as members of the Finnish Government. Orpo was not yet on vacation then, and Multala's vacation officially began only the Monday after Ruisrock. Before the event, guests attended a city- and mayor-hosted gathering at the Radisson Blu Marina Palace hotel. Karoliina Hidén, Communications Director for the City of Turku, says the event, held alongside Ruisrock, is part of the city’s ongoing advocacy and stakeholder engagement. According to IL, the stakeholder event included a buffet lunch with wine and light alcoholic beverages, valued at 65.74 euros per person. There was no limit on alcohol served. Each VIP festival ticket was valued at 339 euros, but according to Hidén, they came at no extra cost to the city, as Ruisrock annually provides the city with a set number of tickets under a cooperation agreement. Guests also received 26 euros worth of drink and food tickets for use at the festival, with any additional purchases at their own expense. Orpo has declared the value of his Ruisrock ticket package as 864.84 euros, while Multala has yet to submit her declaration to Parliament. By the end of July, just over half of the MPs and ministers who received invitation tickets had filed their gift declarations. All declarations must be submitted by the end of August. MPs must declare gifts, tickets, or travel worth over 400 euros. Invitations below that can go unreported, though some disclose them voluntarily. Other ministers who accepted Ruisrock tickets include Minister of Employment Matias Marttinen (NCP) and Minister of Youth, Sport and Physical Activity Mika Poutala (CD). MP Wille Rydman (Finns) was still serving as Minister of Economic Affairs at the time of his invitation. Nearly 60,000 Finns have signed a European Citizens' Initiative focused on the future of video games, Ilta-Sanomat reports. The "Stop Destroying Videogames" initiative calls on publishers selling or licensing games in the EU to keep them functional and playable even after official support ends. Many titles rely on online connections to publishers, which are often severed after server shutdowns — leaving games unplayable and preventing players from restoring them. According to the initiative's appeal, shutting down game servers violates their purchase terms, consumer rights and results in irreversible cultural loss The initiative aimed to gather 9,870 signatures from Finland. With 59,368 Finnish signatures, the country reached 601.5 percent of its national target — the highest proportion in the entire EU. Nearly 1.5 million EU citizens signed the initiative over a year. Headline: Moomin character removed from Brooklyn library exhibition after racism concern
Full_Text: A Moomin character has been dropped from a major exhibition at Brooklyn Public Library in New York after one of the institution's supporters raised concerns that the character might be perceived as racist. "One of their supporters had thought Stinky could be seen as a racist symbol," said Roleff Kråkström, CEO of Moomin Characters, the company that manages the rights to Tove Jansson's beloved Moomin universe. The exhibition, which has drawn a young audience over the summer, features illustrations of Moominvalley characters and details about Jansson's life and work. But Stinky — known in Finnish as Haisuli — was removed from some of the large mural-style displays in the library, although he still appears in the original books on show. Kråkström told Yle he was informed of the decision via a short email from the library and responded with understanding. "We replied in a few lines and said it's fine. We see this as a healthy societal discussion. If such a change is requested, we have no objection," he said. He noted this is the first time in 80 years that the character has drawn such criticism. "Tove Jansson is widely seen as a champion of tolerance, radical acceptance, and inclusivity. But I greatly respect the American sensitivity around these types of conversations," he said. The decision was first reported by Finland's Swedish-language Hufvudstadsbladet newspaper. Sirke Happonen, a Moomin scholar and author of a doctoral dissertation on the Moomin books, said she was surprised by the removal. "It seems sudden and, frankly, absurd," she told Yle. Happonen said the critique appears to be based on Stinky's appearance and "first impression." She argued the character is far from racist and that the decision likely reflects a lack of familiarity with the Moomin stories. "If someone sees Stinky as racist, they haven't really read the comics. I doubt the critic even knows the Moomin stories," she said. "The Moomin world is complex and interesting. People should really dive into it before passing judgment." Stinky is portrayed as a mischievous troublemaker in Moominvalley — often feared by children but also beloved for his antics. "He's quite funny, clearly the rogue of Moominvalley and unapologetically himself," Happonen said. "He lives on rocks in the forest and doesn't have a fixed home, but he's content with his life." The Brooklyn exhibition, the first in the United States to focus on Tove Jansson and the Moomins, has proven popular — especially among younger audiences. The New York Times has covered the show, noting the Moomins' rise in popularity in the US, akin to the cultural impact of Peanuts character Snoopy. The Moomins have recently appeared in fashion collaborations with brands like Acne Studios and Comme des Garçons. The Brooklyn exhibition remains open until 30 September. Yle has reached out to Brooklyn Public Library for comment but has not received a response.

Headline: UK newspaper dubs Finland's Lonkero the 'drink of the summer'
Full_Text: Finland's long drink has become popular in the UK, particularly in the city of Norwich as well as in "pockets of London and Edinburgh", according to UK newspaper The Guardian. In her search for the drink of the summer, The Guardian's Elle Hunt claimed that that title should be bestowed upon a beverage "obvious and undeniable" and lamented the trend cycles emerging from TikTok liked smoked beers and rosorange wine. "So I was taken aback – and a little delighted – when the drink of this summer made itself known to me as though it were the year 2015, not 2025: organically, insistently and right on time. It’s Lonkero: gin mixed with grapefruit soda, available on draught and served in pints," Hunt wrote. She said she tasted a long drink made by a British company called Lonkero Drinks after her friends recommended it. According to the article, Joe Harris, the co-founder of Lonkero Drinks, acquired a taste for the Finnish specialty while working in Helsinki. The drink is doing "surprisingly well" in the city of Norwich, according to Paige Gibbons, the other co-founder of Lonkero Drinks. In addition to Norwich, the company's long drinks are sold in Edinburgh, Brighton, London and other cities. The long drink was created in 1952 as a ready-to-drink mixture of gin and grapefruit juice in order for restaurant staff to quickly serve thirsty visitors to the Helsinki Summer Olympics. Many brands produce long drinks these days in Finland and in the United States as well.

Headline: World's oldest tango festival opens in Seinäjoki
Full_Text: The annual Seinäjoki Tango Festival begins on Wednesday, with an estimated 50,000 people expected to attend the world's oldest event of its kind. The festival — Tangomarkkinat in Finnish — has been running since 1985, and it is widely renowned for including the coronation of a 'Tango King and Queen'. This year, for the first time, festival attendees will pick the Tango royalty from a shortlist of hopefuls — instead of the decision being made by a panel of judges. Although originating from Argentina, tango — an expressive dance and musical style — has been embraced by Finns since the early part of the last century. Pasi Ojala, CEO of the Seinäjoki festival, told Yle that the festival has been slowly recovering its popularity after the Covid pandemic. "Since the coronavirus crisis, we have managed to get our finances in order and run the event with our own funds, and there have been good years and bad years," he said, adding that a weather forecast of warm temperatures and little to no rain should help matters. Headline: Moomins turn 80 with anniversary shows in New York and Tampere
Full_Text: An exhibition on Finnish artist and author Tove Jansson and her Moominvalley characters has opened in New York City. The Moomin 80th anniversary show is on display at the Brooklyn Public Library until the end of September. Tove Jansson and the Moomins: The Door Is Always Open is the first major exhibition in the United States to presenting Jansson's life and Moomin characters. It offers an in-depth look at Jansson's career, life and the world of the Moomins through texts, archival materials, books and events. These include readings, animated film screenings and panel discussions. The exhibition is a collaboration between Moomin Characters and the City of Tampere, as well as corporate partners Arabia and Finnair. The exhibition notes that the original illustrations and three-dimensional dioramas donated by Jansson can be seen at the world's only Moomin Museum in Tampere. Tampere will also host a Moomin exhibition celebrating the 80th anniversary of the publication of the first Moomin story. "The most important international investment of the anniversary year is the collaboration on the Tove Jansson and the Moomins exhibition, with which we present the Moomin Museum and Tampere to the world," Tampere marketing director Iina Ojala said in a press release. The Tampere show focuses on the original Moomin House model and its three-year construction process. The exhibition is on display until the end of August at the Moomin Museum in Tampere Hall. In December, the first US exhibition featuring another iconic Finnish artist, Helene Schjerfbeck, opens at the Metropolitan Museum in New York.
